title: Failover
concept: Failover is how a system keeps serving when a component dies: detect the failure, promote or route to a healthy stand-in, and send clients to the new target, all fast enough that users barely notice. The hard parts are detecting a real failure without being fooled by a slow network, choosing exactly one replacement so you never end up with two primaries (split-brain), and redirecting traffic without waiting on slow caches or DNS. Failover spans tiers: a database promotes a replica to primary, and a load balancer routes around an unhealthy server, but both are the same loop of detect, decide, redirect. A third approach prepares spare capacity in advance so little has to be detected and decided at the moment of failure.

points: Failover keeps a system serving when a component dies: detect the failure, promote or route to a stand-in, and send clients to it.
The hard parts are not being fooled by a slow network, choosing exactly one replacement so there is no split-brain, and redirecting without waiting on caches.
GitHub splits database failover into detecting without false positives, deciding once with consensus, and redirecting through a proxy instead of DNS.
Amazon's static stability argues the best recovery step is one that does not have to happen, so spare capacity is held in other zones.

thirtySeconds: Failover turns spare copies into real availability: detect a failure, pick one replacement, and redirect work to it. I confirm a failure with several observers, promote exactly one replica, and fence the old primary so it cannot cause split brain. Clients move through a proxy I control rather than waiting on DNS time to live. Acting on one missed health check causes needless failovers. GitHub's 2018 post reports a total outage of 10 to 13 seconds in most failover cases.

prerequisiteReasons.replication: Failover takes from replication the standby copies that are already current enough to be promoted when the primary dies.
prerequisiteReasons.consensus: Failover takes from consensus the way to choose exactly one replacement, since only one backed by a majority may take over.
prerequisiteReasons.circuit-breakers: Failover takes from circuit breakers the habit of treating a failing dependency as down and routing around it instead of waiting on it.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why redundancy alone is not availability, and what failover adds.
why.body:
Replication gives you spare copies, but spares do not help if nothing switches to them. If a database has one primary that takes writes and the primary dies, the replicas are useless for writing until one is promoted. If a service has three servers and one goes down, traffic keeps hitting the dead one until something stops sending it there. Redundancy is potential availability; failover is what turns it into actual availability.

Failover is a loop with three steps: detect that a component has failed, decide on a healthy replacement, and redirect work to it. Each step is harder than it sounds. Detection must distinguish a truly dead node from a slow or briefly unreachable one, or it will fail over needlessly and cause the outage it meant to prevent. The decision must pick exactly one replacement, because two nodes both believing they are the primary, split-brain, can corrupt data. And redirection must take effect quickly, which is hard when clients cache the old address. Getting all three right, fast, is the whole topic.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture the detect, decide, redirect loop and where split-brain threatens it.
mentalModel.body:
Picture a primary and its replicas, plus a watcher observing them. The watcher continuously health-checks the primary. When checks fail, the watcher must answer: is the primary really dead, or just slow? To avoid being fooled, good systems ask several vantage points (separate places to watch from) and act only when they agree, rather than trusting a single missed check or a single observer, which is why failover and consensus are close relatives.

Once the watcher is confident, it promotes one replica to primary. This is a leader election, and it must yield exactly one winner, so it is typically backed by a quorum: only a replacement that a majority agrees on is allowed to take over, which prevents two primaries. Finally, clients must find the new primary. If they rely on DNS (the lookup that turns a name into an address) with a time-to-live (how long an answer may be cached), they may keep using the old address until the cache expires, so fast systems redirect at a layer they control, a load balancer or proxy, rather than waiting on a cache. The fencing of the old primary, making sure it cannot still accept writes, is the subtle safety step that stops split-brain. A different approach holds spare capacity ready in advance, so a failure needs nothing launched or changed at that moment; this is called static stability.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through detection, promotion, fencing, and client redirection, and why each guards against a failure mode.

steps.explanation: A monitor probes each component on an interval, checking not just that the process is up but that it is actually serving. What counts as healthy is defined per system, for example a successful query or an HTTP 200.

steps.step: Confirm the failure with multiple observers
steps.explanation: To avoid acting on a slow network or a single bad vantage point, treat a failure as real only when several observers agree, for example when all of a primary's replicas report they cannot reach it. This is holistic detection.

Promote one replica to primary through a decision that cannot pick two, usually a quorum or consensus leader. Choosing the most up-to-date replica minimises data loss when replication was asynchronous.

Ensure the failed primary cannot still accept writes if it comes back or was only partitioned, by revoking its lease, taking its address, or stopping it. Without fencing, two primaries can accept conflicting writes: split-brain.
Point clients at the new target through a layer you control, a proxy or load balancer, rather than relying on DNS time-to-live, so traffic moves in seconds instead of waiting for caches to expire.

Attach a fresh replica to restore the failure budget (how many more failures you can survive), and rate-limit repeated failovers so a flapping component (one that keeps switching between up and down) does not trigger a storm of promotions.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace a database primary failure through promotion and redirection, and see where split-brain is prevented.

steps.explanation: A MySQL cluster has one primary taking writes and several replicas replaying its changes and serving reads, spread across data centres.
A monitor's health checks to the primary start failing. Rather than acting on its own view, it treats the primary as failed only when the replicas also agree they cannot reach it.

A failover controller, backed by consensus so only one decision is made, promotes the most up-to-date replica to primary. Because replication was asynchronous, picking the furthest-ahead replica minimises lost writes.

The old primary should be fenced so it cannot accept writes if it returns (GitHub sets it read-only when it can, and says a short period of split-brain is still possible in a data centre isolation), and the new primary's identity is published to a proxy layer. Clients, which only ever knew a name routed through the proxy, now reach the new primary without a DNS wait.
In GitHub's design, which promotes through a raft leader and redirects through a proxy instead of DNS, total outage was 10 to 13 seconds in most cases, not minutes.

steps.step: A slow network, not a death
steps.explanation: If instead the primary were merely slow for two seconds, requiring agreement across observers prevents a needless failover, avoiding the self-inflicted outage of promoting while the real primary is still alive.

quiz.question: Why is replication alone not enough for high availability?
options: Replicas are only for backups, never for serving
Spare copies do nothing unless something detects a failure and switches traffic to them
quiz.why: Redundancy is only potential availability; failover is the mechanism that detects the failure and promotes or routes to a healthy copy, turning spares into real availability.
wrong: Replication copies data. Detecting failure and redirecting clients is what failover adds.
Replicas commonly serve reads and become the new primary on failover, so they are not only backups.

quiz.question: Why confirm a failure with multiple observers before failing over?
options: To avoid being fooled by a slow or briefly unreachable node and failing over needlessly
To make the health checks run faster
Because one observer cannot send a health check
quiz.why: A single missed check can mean a slow network, not a dead node; requiring several vantage points to agree prevents a needless failover that would cause its own outage.
wrong: More observers raise confidence that the failure is real.
One observer can run a check, but its view alone is too unreliable to act on.

quiz.question: What is split-brain, and what prevents it during failover?
options: Replicas falling so far behind the primary that reads go stale; fixed by upgrading to faster replication links
Two active primaries taking conflicting writes; prevented by electing one winner and fencing the old one
The monitor crashing so that no failover can happen; fixed by running more monitors in more zones
quiz.why: If the old primary keeps accepting writes while a new one is promoted, both diverge; a quorum picks exactly one and fencing stops the old one from writing.
wrong: Split-brain is about two primaries, not lagging replicas.
A crashed monitor is a different problem; split-brain is specifically two active primaries.

quiz.question: Why do fast systems redirect clients through a proxy or load balancer instead of DNS?
options: Because DNS cannot store IP addresses, so every redirect needs a proxy that keeps its own address table
Because clients may cache a DNS record until its TTL expires, delaying the switch
Because proxies are cheaper to run than DNS
quiz.why: DNS answers are cached for their time-to-live, so clients can keep using the dead address for seconds or minutes; a controlled proxy layer moves traffic immediately.
wrong: DNS stores addresses fine; the problem is caching and TTLs.
The reason is avoiding the delay of waiting for cached DNS to expire; cost plays no part.

quiz.question: During an asynchronous-replication failover, which replica should be promoted to minimise data loss?
options: Any replica at random, since every replica is equally current once a failure has been detected
The one with the least traffic, because it has the most spare capacity to take over
The most up-to-date replica, the one furthest ahead in applying the primary's changes
quiz.why: With asynchronous replication some replicas lag; promoting the furthest-ahead one loses the fewest acknowledged writes.
wrong: A random replica might be far behind, losing more writes than necessary.
Traffic level does not indicate how current a replica's data is.

quiz.question: Why rate-limit or dampen repeated failovers?
options: So a flapping node does not trigger a storm of back-to-back promotions
To make failover slower on purpose, so operators always have time to approve each promotion by hand
Because failover is only allowed once per cluster ever, after which the cluster becomes read-only
quiz.why: A node that flaps up and down could cause back-to-back failovers, each disruptive; an anti-flapping delay lets things settle before failing over again.
wrong: The aim is stability, and a real failure still fails over promptly.
Failover can happen many times over a cluster's life; it is just damped against flapping.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how a database tier fails over by detecting and reacting, and how static stability prepares spare capacity so nothing has to react.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can tell apart detecting and reacting to a failure, as GitHub does, and pre-provisioning capacity so that little has to react, as the AWS article describes.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can design detection that avoids false positives, prevent split-brain, and plan cross-region failover.

exercises.prompt: A single-primary database fails over whenever one monitor misses two health checks, and it keeps failing over during brief network blips, causing more downtime than the blips would. Fix the detection.
exercises.answer: Stop acting on a single observer. Require agreement from multiple vantage points, for example the primary's own replicas reporting they cannot reach it, before declaring a failure (holistic detection). Add a short confirmation window and an anti-flapping cooldown so a recovered node does not immediately trigger another failover. A true death still fails over quickly, but a two-second blip no longer does.
exercises.tradeoffs: Requiring agreement adds a little detection latency before a real failover, in exchange for far fewer false positives. The cooldown briefly blocks a second failover, which is almost always what you want.
wrongAnswers: Shorten the health-check interval so it reacts even faster to blips.
Fail over on the first missed check from any single monitor.
Disable failover entirely to stop the flapping.

exercises.prompt: Design failover for a single-writer database so that a promotion never results in two primaries, even if the old primary was only network-partitioned and later returns.
exercises.answer: Make promotion a single, quorum-backed decision: only a replacement a majority agrees on may take over, so two primaries can never both be elected. Fence the old primary before or as the new one takes writes, by revoking its lease, removing its proxy entry, or stopping its write port, so a returning partitioned primary cannot accept writes. Route clients through a proxy whose backend is the elected primary, so a stale primary is simply not reachable as the write target.
exercises.tradeoffs: Quorum promotion means a failover needs a majority reachable, so a cluster that has lost its majority will not promote, blocking writes rather than risking split-brain. Fencing adds a step and must itself be reliable, but it is the price of never corrupting data.
wrongAnswers: Let any replica promote itself when it stops hearing the primary.
Skip fencing and assume the old primary stays down.
Rely on DNS TTL to eventually stop traffic to the old primary.

exercises.prompt: Your service runs on a fleet in one Region across three Availability Zones (separate data centres within the Region), and traffic grows tenfold. Today, when a zone is impaired, you rely on Auto Scaling to launch replacement instances in the other zones. How do you change the design so a zone failure needs no reaction, and what does it cost?
exercises.answer: Provision for the failure in advance instead of reacting to it. Keep the fleet across three or more zones and size it so the instances in any two zones can carry the full load; the AWS article's example is 50 percent extra capacity with three zones, so each zone runs at about 66 percent of its load-tested level. Put the fleet behind a load balancer with health checks, so when a zone is impaired its instances fail checks and traffic shifts to the others with no launches. For the primary database, keep a warm standby in a different zone so promotion needs no new infrastructure, and for a cluster with a leader elect the new leader from a standby candidate instead of launching one just in time.
exercises.tradeoffs: You pay for spare capacity all the time, and every zone is deliberately underused. In return a zone failure needs no control plane action and no instance start-up steps, which are the things most likely to misbehave during an impairment. As traffic grows tenfold the spare capacity grows with it, so the cost grows too, and the article notes that gray failures a load balancer cannot see still need other handling.
wrongAnswers: Size the fleet for normal load and count on Auto Scaling to launch enough replacements after a zone fails.
Run everything in one zone to keep the design simple and avoid cross-zone traffic.
Add more instances only after a zone shows errors, since idle capacity is wasted money.

next.outcome: After this you can see how failover ties the reliability topics together.
next.body: Failover builds on three topics. Replication provides the stand-ins. Consensus supplies the promotion step, electing exactly one new primary. Circuit Breakers and health checks decide what counts as failed, and the detection step has to cope with the same ambiguity between a slow node and a dead one. Together these are how a system stays available through failure. Disaster Recovery and Backups picks up from there, for the failures failover cannot cover: lost data, and the loss of a whole site. Traffic Steering and Draining covers a different follow-on: how traffic is moved once the decision is made, and why the layer you move it with sets the speed.

posts.title: MySQL High Availability at GitHub
posts.ageNote: From June 2018 (the page also shows an update in May 2020), included for a fundamental that has not changed: how to fail a single-writer database over in seconds by detecting failure holistically, promoting with consensus, and redirecting clients through a controlled layer instead of DNS. GitHub's exact stack has evolved since, so treat the figures (such as 10 to 13 seconds) as of the post and the detect-promote-redirect design as the lasting lesson.

digest.problem: GitHub runs multiple MySQL clusters in a classic primary-replicas setup: one primary accepts writes, replicas replay its changes asynchronously and serve reads. If the primary fails, writes stop until a replica is promoted, so GitHub needed automated failover that is fast, loses little or no data, works across data centres, and never produces two primaries.
digest.constraints: The previous design used Orchestrator for detection and failover but VIP and DNS for clients to find the primary, which had bad failure modes: VIP reassignment can split-brain, waiting to contact the dead primary to release its VIP wastes time, and DNS time-to-live means clients keep resolving the old address. The new design had to remove the DNS and VIP dependency and work cleanly across data centres.

walkthrough.explanation: Orchestrator does not trust a single probe. It triages by multiple observers, the replication topology servers themselves; when all of a primary's replicas agree they cannot contact it, the topology is broken de-facto and a failover is justified.

GitHub runs a cross-data-centre orchestrator/raft setup: the Orchestrator nodes communicate by Raft consensus, so failover is driven by the single raft leader and the decision is agreed, not made independently by many actors.
On a confirmed primary failure the orchestrator/raft leader promotes a replica to primary and begins fixing the replication tree beneath it.

walkthrough.step: Discover the new primary through Consul
walkthrough.explanation: Instead of VIP and DNS, GitHub uses HashiCorp Consul for service discovery. Orchestrator writes the new primary's identity into Consul's key-value store, and propagates that change to all its nodes via Raft so every data centre learns it.

Applications connect to write nodes through GLB/HAProxy, so discovery, as far as the apps are concerned, ends at the proxy. When Consul is updated, the proxy backends change; clients never need to re-resolve a name or wait for a DNS cache.

digest.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" role="img" aria-labelledby="dg-ghmy-t" class="dg"><title id="dg-ghmy-t">GitHub MySQL failover: an orchestrator/raft cluster detects a dead primary when its replicas agree they cannot reach it, the raft leader promotes a replica, writes the new primary into Consul and propagates it by raft, and apps reach the primary through GLB/HAProxy so no DNS TTL wait is needed; total outage is typically 10 to 13 seconds.</title><defs><marker id="dg-ghmy-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><rect x="18" y="120" width="120" height="48" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="78" y="140" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">orchestrator</text><text x="78" y="157" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">/raft leader</text><rect x="18" y="40" width="120" height="40" class="dg-box" opacity="0.5"/><text x="78" y="64.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">primary (dead)</text><rect x="18" y="210" width="132" height="38" class="dg-box"/><text x="84" y="233.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">replica -> primary</text><path d="M78,120 L78,80" class="dg-line dg-dashed" marker-end="url(#dg-ghmy-a)"/><text x="86" y="104" class="dg-note" text-anchor="start">replicas agree: dead</text><path d="M78,168 L78,210" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-ghmy-a)"/><text x="86" y="192" class="dg-note" text-anchor="start">promote</text><rect x="230" y="120" width="110" height="48" class="dg-box"/><text x="285" y="150.5" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">Consul KV</text><path d="M138,140 L230,142" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-ghmy-a)"/><text x="184" y="132" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">write primary</text><rect x="410" y="120" width="132" height="48" class="dg-box"/><text x="476" y="140" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">GLB / HAProxy</text><text x="476" y="157" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">apps connect here</text><path d="M340,144 L410,144" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-ghmy-a)"/><text x="280" y="284" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">no VIP, no DNS TTL wait: typically 10 to 13 seconds of total outage</text></svg>

numbers.meaning: Total outage time in most failover cases with the orchestrator/raft plus Consul plus GLB design
Total outage in less frequent (20 seconds) and extreme (25 seconds) cases

numbers.value: a single node in a cluster
numbers.meaning: The primary: the one node in a cluster that is able to accept writes; failover must promote exactly one replacement

tradeoffs.chosen: Holistic, replica-corroborated failure detection; a cross-DC orchestrator/raft consensus controller for promotion; Consul plus GLB/HAProxy for client discovery, removing VIP and DNS.
tradeoffs.rejected: The earlier VIP-and-DNS discovery, which risked split-brain on VIP reassignment, wasted time contacting the dead primary, and left clients waiting on DNS time-to-live.
tradeoffs.why: VIP and DNS tied failover speed to cache expiry and to co-locating servers, and could leave two hosts claiming one VIP. Moving discovery into Consul fed by orchestrator/raft lets GitHub fail over across data centres without a DNS wait and with a single agreed decision, bringing most failovers to 10 to 13 seconds.

digest.failures: The post is candid about the old design's failure modes it set out to kill: VIP reassignment split-brain, the wasted step of asking a dead primary to release its VIP, and DNS TTL delaying client cutover, with cross-DC failover especially slow. The new design still has limits it names: the proxy hides the application's identity from the primary, a data centre isolation can leave a short period of split-brain until a planned STONITH is in place, and a Consul outage during a failover is an unhandled scenario.
digest.takeaways: Fast database failover is three problems, not one: detect without false positives (corroborate across replicas), decide once (consensus-backed promotion), and redirect without waiting on caches (a proxy fed by service discovery, not DNS). GitHub's setup does all three and reports 10 to 13 seconds of total outage in most cases; our own reading is that this is why failover leans on both replication and consensus.

posts.title: Static stability using Availability Zones
posts.ageNote: No year is recorded. The page shows "Published Oct 2, 2026" and "Last modified Oct 2, 2026", which looks like a republication of an older article, so the real age is unknown. It is here for a fundamental: prepare capacity before a failure instead of reacting to it. The page describes how Amazon builds its services, in the author's words, and any opinions in it may not reflect AWS's. Treat its details as that article's account, and do not assume they describe AWS today.

digest.problem: AWS services must meet very high availability targets, and every one of them depends on Availability Zones, which are logically isolated sections of a Region built to operate independently. The article asks how to build on that so a service keeps working when a zone, or any dependency, becomes impaired. Its answer is a pattern called static stability: the system keeps working even when a dependency is impaired, because everything it was doing before continues to work.
digest.constraints: The article contrasts two ways to use several zones. A less effective one is to deploy to multiple zones and, if one is impaired, scale up in the others, for example with Auto Scaling. That depends on reacting as the impairment happens, which means taking an immediate dependency on the EC2 control plane and on every application-specific step a new instance needs, such as downloading configuration, registering with discovery and acquiring credentials. Stateful services add a further constraint: a relational database has one primary that takes all writes.

walkthrough.explanation: The article's lesson is to be ready for impairments before they happen. A statically stable service overprovisions its infrastructure until it would keep operating correctly without launching any new EC2 instances, even if a zone became impaired.

walkthrough.step: Spread across three or more zones with spare room
walkthrough.explanation: For stateless services the article describes an Auto Scaling group across three or more zones, overprovisioned so the servers in the remaining zones can carry the load if an entire zone is impaired. With three zones that means 50 percent extra, so each zone runs at only 66 percent of the level it was load-tested for.

walkthrough.step: Do nothing when a zone fails
walkthrough.explanation: In the load-balanced example no action is needed: the instances in the impaired zone start failing health checks and the Application Load Balancer shifts traffic away from them. For a fleet reading from a queue the article says the service does nothing, because the impaired instances stop working and others pick up the slack.

walkthrough.step: Keep a warm standby for stateful services
walkthrough.explanation: For a service with a single primary the article puts a warm standby in a different zone. When the primary's zone is impaired, the service does nothing with the infrastructure: for Amazon RDS, RDS manages the failover and repoints the DNS name to the new primary in the working zone. Clusters with a leader are deployed across zones and elect the new leader from a standby candidate instead of launching a replacement just in time.

walkthrough.step: Separate the control plane from the data plane
walkthrough.explanation: The article says the control plane is the machinery for making changes, such as launching an instance, and the data plane is the daily business of the resources. The EC2 data plane is designed to stay statically stable if the control plane is impaired: the physical machine has local access to what it needs to route packets, so traffic that worked before keeps working, though it may not see new updates.

For foundational building blocks the article goes further: deployments follow a zonal calendar so a bad change affects one zone, packet flows stay inside their zone, and the NAT gateway is a zonal service. It accepts the extra complexity of managing zonal rather than regional resources in return.

numbers.meaning: Extra capacity the article says it overprovisions when it uses three Availability Zones, so the remaining zones can carry the load
The level of its load-tested capacity at which each zone then runs, in the article's three-zone example

The chance a request avoids an impaired zone when one regional service calls another (2/3 x 2/3 = 4/9), versus a zonal service called from the same zone (2/3); for N services the article gives (2/3)^N versus 2/3

tradeoffs.chosen: Provision all capacity needed for a zone impairment in advance, so that neither stateless fleets nor stateful clusters need to launch new infrastructure or modify anything in response.
tradeoffs.rejected: Deploying across several zones and scaling up in the surviving zones after an impairment, which the article calls less effective because it relies on reacting as impairments happen.
tradeoffs.why: The article says a reactive design takes an immediate dependency for its recovery path on the EC2 control plane and on application-specific steps, and that control plane systems are more complex and more likely to misbehave when the overall system is impaired. A service that already has the capacity needs none of that at the moment of failure.

digest.failures: The article gives no incident or failure account of its own. It names a failure mode it designs around: gray failures, such as software bugs that a load balancer cannot see in its health check, which is one reason it keeps foundational services zonal. It also states the costs of its choices: additional complexity, for example managing zonal rather than regional service environments, or running multiple NAT gateways and route tables per zone, and states the 50 percent overprovision without discussing what that spare capacity costs.
digest.takeaways: The best recovery step is one that does not have to happen. By holding spare capacity in other zones, a stateless service can lose a zone without launching anything, and a stateful service can promote a standby that already exists. The article's own summary is that the key to static stability is to anticipate impairments before they happen.

comparison:
Both posts are about keeping a service up when part of it fails, and both reach the same practical conclusion: do not make recovery depend on something slow or fragile at the moment of failure. GitHub's post is about a stateful single-writer database; the AWS article is about building on Availability Zones, mostly for stateless fleets, with a short section on stateful ones.

Where they diverge is when the work happens. GitHub detects and reacts: orchestrator and Raft decide that the primary is dead and promote exactly one replica, and a proxy fed by Consul redirects clients. The AWS article argues for pre-provisioning: capacity for a zone impairment is already running, so the load balancer simply shifts traffic and nothing is launched. For stateful services the article still has a failover, since RDS repoints a DNS name and a standby is elected as leader, but the standby already exists and nothing new is provisioned in response.

The evidence differs too. GitHub reports total outage of 10 to 13 seconds in most cases, up to 20 to 25 in rarer ones. The AWS article gives no recovery times; it gives capacity arithmetic, 50 percent extra with three zones and each zone at 66 percent of its tested level, and the odds of a request avoiding an impaired zone, 4/9 for two regional services in a row against 2/3 for zonal ones. It is a republished page with no date to rely on, and it describes Amazon's own practice, so read it as one company's account of a pattern.

glossary.definition: Detecting a failed component and switching to a healthy stand-in so the system keeps serving.
A periodic probe that decides whether a component is actually serving, not just running.
Turning a replica into the new primary when the old primary fails.
Two nodes both acting as primary and taking conflicting writes; failover must prevent it.

glossary.definition: Ensuring a failed or partitioned primary cannot still accept writes, by revoking its lease or address.

glossary.definition: Declaring a failure only when multiple observers (such as the primary's replicas) agree, to avoid false positives.
A system (such as Consul) that tells clients, via a proxy, which node is currently the primary.
How long a DNS answer is cached; relying on it makes failover wait for caches to expire.
A design that keeps working when a dependency is impaired because the capacity and state it needs are already in place, so nothing has to be launched or changed in response.

The control plane is the machinery for making changes, such as launching an instance; the data plane is the daily work of the running resources. Keeping the data plane working without the control plane is the heart of static stability.

mistakes: Failing over on a single missed health check. A slow or briefly unreachable node looks dead to one observer; acting on that alone causes needless failovers, so confirm with multiple observers before promoting.

Forgetting to fence the old primary. If the failed primary returns or was only partitioned and keeps accepting writes while a new one is promoted, you get split-brain and divergent data; promotion must be a single quorum-backed decision plus fencing.
Relying on DNS time-to-live to redirect clients. Clients cache DNS answers and may ignore short TTLs, so traffic keeps hitting the dead target; redirect through a proxy or edge you control instead.
